source.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
source.authors: Mark Muchane; Sean M. Richardson; Kiho Park; Victor Veitch

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether sparse autoencoders recover interpretable, hierarchically organized features from a real LLM, using a new hierarchical SAE architecture rather than the original toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own SAE reconstruction, feature-absorption, cross-language feature-overlap, and qualitative hierarchy results. Results cited from other work are not included. Hyperparameters and model sizes used to configure experiments are not results.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE architecture paper. It uses sparse dictionary learning on Gemma 2-2B as a tool and reports how its hierarchical SAE performs against a TopK SAE baseline: reconstruction, absorption, cross-language redundancy and qualitative examples. It does not test whether Gemma's representations are in superposition or whether SAE features are the model's canonical or one-dimensional units. All quantitative results compare the study's own method with another method. The hierarchical, low-dimensional subspace structure is assumed from prior work (Park et al.) and built into the architecture, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say hierarchy dramatically improves reconstruction, moderately improves interpretability of top-level features, yields learned hierarchical semantics, and greatly improves compute efficiency. They also note results remain imperfect: some features are hard to interpret and reconstruction falls far short of perfect.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces a hierarchical sparse autoencoder for Gemma 2-2B rather than reproducing the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are shown across top-level dictionary sizes and H-SAE sublatent counts; cross-language feature similarity is reported separately for six language pairs.

fits_no_version.finding: A hierarchical SAE (top-level features plus low-dimensional expert sub-SAEs) beats a TopK SAE on Gemma 2-2B layer-20 reconstruction, first-letter absorption and cross-language redundancy. Examples: EN-FR set difference 8.448 vs 9.772; FR-DE 7.306 vs 9.038.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE architectures that encode hierarchical, subspace-structured concepts recover LLM features with less absorption and redundancy than flat SAEs.

record.problems: Evidence is from one LLM and one stated residual-stream layer for the main experiments. Hierarchy is assessed qualitatively, and the authors note that some features remain hard to interpret and reconstruction remains imperfect. Figure-only reconstruction and absorption plots do not provide extractable numeric values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result relevant to the tested version was left out.

untested.parts: No toy models, no superposition geometry, no sparsity transition.
No test of capacity competition or neuron polysemanticity.
No test of non-capacity sources of polysemanticity.
Does not measure how features spread over neurons, or whether the model contains sparse features. SAE recoverability is presupposed, not tested.
Does not test completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features. Only compares two SAE architectures on absorption and redundancy.
Assumes hierarchical concepts occupy low-dimensional subspaces (from Park et al.) and builds this into the architecture. Does not test whether superposed features are 1-D.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with V4 'supports' is not justified: every quantitative row compares the study's own method with a baseline. The baseline TopK SAE's absolute absorption (about 0.3-0.6) and cross-language redundancy might be read as weak evidence against V5 canonicity. However, the paper does not frame or test it that way. The ablations on whitened unembeddings are qualitative only.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, superposition geometry, or a sparsity-dependent transition.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons result from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test non-capacity mechanisms for polysemantic neurons.

Tests SAE-derived features and their reconstruction, interpretability proxies, and qualitative hierarchy in Gemma 2-2B; does not establish that these are ground-truth sparse features or measure how features are distributed across neurons.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model.
Uses a hierarchical architecture with low-dimensional subspaces, but does not test whether the model's superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional features.
